Yes — demand exceeded the contract limit on the morning of 16 June 2025.

- **Peak demand:** 1,324.4 kW at 08:15, which is 106% of the 1,250 kW contract limit [data: get_demand].
- **Intervals over contract:** 2 — 08:00 at 1,307.1 kW and 08:15 at 1,324.4 kW [data: get_demand].
- **Cause:** This is the "Monday morning simultaneous start" scenario (S2) — demand climbed from ~320 kW before 07:15 to a spike of 1,307 kW at 08:00 as the SMT lines and ovens started together, then settled back to ~1,080 kW for the rest of the morning [data: get_demand].

So yes, it was too high — briefly over the 1,250 kW contract, peaking at 1,324.4 kW.

I have the answer from the plant documents.

## Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby

Per SOP-02 and the EQ-01 Reflow Oven Manual, a reflow oven in **standby draws 36% of its 70 kW rating — about 25.2 kW** — for as long as it stays on, even though it produces nothing. That is a large idle load. A properly **switched-off** oven uses only about 340–350 kWh per oven-weekend (the residual/heat-up energy), so leaving it in standby wastes far more. The rule is: switch ovens off (not standby) for the weekend and holidays, after the 30-minute post-line warm-down and only when no boards are inside [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby].

## Excess energy in incident S5

In incident S5 (2025-10-17 to 2025-10-20), RF-02 was left in standby all weekend. Weekend energy was about **1,556 kWh against about 346 kWh normal**, an excess of about **1,210 kWh from a single oven** [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby].

Note: I can report these figures from the documents, but the exact weekend energy for RF-02 is not independently verified by a measurement tool here — the values come from the incident write-up in SOP-02.

## Load Shedding Order

**Which load is shed first:** According to the restore sequence in SOP-03, loads are restored in reverse order — "pressure, setpoint, burn-in loading, then EV charging" [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 5: restore]. This means **compressed-air pressure is shed first**, followed by setpoint, burn-in loading, and finally EV charging.

**Which loads must never be shed:** Per EM-02 and SOP-03, the following are never part of any load-shed action:
- Server room (DC-01) — a continuous critical load [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Load-shed playbook > Never shed]
- Running molders mid-cycle (IM-01 to IM-04) [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Load-shed playbook > Never shed]
- Reflow ovens with boards inside (RF-01 to RF-03) [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Load-shed playbook > Never shed]

This is confirmed in EM-01's operating principles: "The server room, running molders mid-cycle and reflow ovens with boards inside are never shed" [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-01_energy_policy.md#EM-01 Energy Policy > Operating principles].
